name: Pashupatinath
tagline: Nepal's holiest Shiva temple on the banks of the Bagmati
meta_description: Pashupatinath Temple guide: darshan timings, evening aarti, entry rules for Indians and non-Hindus, Arya Ghat etiquette, Guhyeshwari and Shivaratri.
summary: Pashupatinath is the most sacred Shiva temple in Nepal, set on the Bagmati River 5 km east of central Kathmandu and 2 km from the airport. Hindus come for darshan of the four-faced lingam and the evening aarti; visitors of other faiths watch the ghats, cremations and rituals respectfully from the east bank.
intro: For Hindus from Nepal and India, Pashupatinath is one of the great pilgrimages of the subcontinent, often paired with Kedarnath and Kashi Vishwanath. Shiva is worshipped here as Pashupati, lord of all living beings, in a black stone lingam with four faces, housed in a two-roofed pagoda with gilded roofs and silver-plated doors. A great golden Nandi faces the shrine. The temple's chief priests have for centuries come from Karnataka in south India, a tradition linked to Adi Shankaracharya, and they alone touch the main lingam during the daily rituals.

The complex is far larger than the main temple. Shrines, lingams, sadhu shelters, rest houses and smaller temples spread along both banks of the Bagmati, and the wooded hill of Mrigasthali rises on the east side, where monkeys and spotted deer live in the forest. Downstream of the temple, open-air cremations take place on stone platforms at Arya Ghat and Bhasmeshwar Ghat throughout the day. The site is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1979, and it came through the 2015 earthquake with the main shrine intact.

Entry rules matter here. Only Hindus may enter the main temple courtyard; the rule is enforced at the gates, and visitors of other faiths, including Buddhists of non-Nepali origin, watch from the terraces across the river, which actually give the best view of the roofs and the ghats. Indian and Nepali Hindus enter free for darshan, while foreign visitors pay around NPR 1,000 for the wider complex; check current status before you travel. We plan most visits for late afternoon, so the walk around the ghats ends with the evening aarti.
facts: Oct – Mar; Maha Shivaratri in Feb or Mar
≈ 5 km from Thamel · 20–40 min by car
Pashupati lingam, Bagmati aarti, Arya Ghat, Guhyeshwari

highlights.title: Darshan of the Pashupati lingam
highlights.text: Hindu pilgrims queue through the west gate into the main courtyard for darshan of the four-faced lingam, each face looking to a cardinal direction. Mornings from about 4 am and Mondays bring the longest lines; mid-morning on a weekday is usually calmer. Phones, cameras and leather goods stay outside the courtyard.

highlights.title: Evening aarti on the Bagmati
highlights.text: Every evening, around 6 pm in summer and earlier in winter, priests perform the Bagmati aarti with lamps, conch shells, bells and bhajans on the river steps. Devotees and visitors fill the stone terraces on the east bank. It lasts about an hour and is free to watch; check current timings before you travel.

highlights.title: The cremation ghats
highlights.text: Families bring their dead to the stone platforms at Arya Ghat and Bhasmeshwar Ghat, wash the body in the river and light the pyre, often with the eldest son leading the rites. Watching from the east bank is accepted. Stay quiet, keep a respectful distance, and do not photograph grieving families or the bodies.

highlights.title: Mrigasthali forest and its temples
highlights.text: Stone steps climb from the east bank into the forest of Mrigasthali, where legend says Shiva wandered as a deer. Monkeys are everywhere, spotted deer graze in an enclosure, and rows of small shrines and lingams line the paths up to the Gorakhnath temple area under the trees. It is a shady escape from the ghats.

highlights.title: Guhyeshwari, the Shakti Peeth
highlights.text: About 1 km upstream along the Bagmati stands Guhyeshwari, one of the Shakti Peethas, where the goddess is worshipped in the form of a sacred pool. Pilgrims usually visit it with Pashupatinath on the same day. As at the main temple, only Hindus may enter the inner courtyard.

highlights.title: Sadhus and festival days
highlights.text: Ash-covered sadhus sit on the east bank all year and arrive in thousands for Maha Shivaratri in February or March. Teej in August or September fills the temple with women in red saris, and on Bala Chaturdashi in November or December families scatter seeds along the forest path for their departed.

how_to_reach.text: Pashupatinath is about 5 km east of Thamel and Durbar Marg, a 20 to 40 minute drive depending on traffic at Chabahil and Gaushala. Most of our guests come by private car with a guide; a metered or negotiated taxi from Thamel costs about NPR 500 to 700. Cars drop you at the Gaushala side for the main gate or at the Mrigasthali side for the east bank.

Tribhuvan International Airport is only about 2 km away, and you can see planes landing over the temple. That makes Pashupatinath an easy first or last stop: pilgrims flying in from Delhi, Varanasi or Mumbai often go straight to darshan, and afternoon departures leave time for a morning visit. Allow 15 minutes by car from the terminal.

From Boudhanath the walk is about 2 km and 30 to 40 minutes through local lanes, crossing the ring road and entering via the Mrigasthali forest on the east bank. Many of our walking tours link the two sites this way, often finishing at the evening aarti. From Guhyeshwari it is 15 minutes along the river.

where_to_stay: There is no hotel strip inside the temple area itself, only simple pilgrim rest houses and guesthouses around Gaushala and Battisputali that suit those who want to reach the 4 am darshan on foot. Dwarika's Hotel in Battisputali is about 1.5 km away and is the most comfortable base close to the temple. Gokarna Forest Resort, a Premium resort set in forest north-east of the city, is about 20 minutes by car and works well for families who want calm after a temple day. Most guests, though, stay in Thamel or Lazimpat, around 5 km west, where 3-star hotels and Hotel Shanker put them near restaurants and shopping.
tips: Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees, and leave belts, wallets and bags made of leather in the car before entering the main temple.
Hire a guide or temple priest only through the official counters, and agree any puja fee before the ritual starts.
Never stand on the cremation platforms or step between a pyre and the river, and keep your camera down near grieving families.
Hold on to sunglasses, flowers and snacks on the Mrigasthali steps, because the monkeys are quick and bold.
Sadhus who pose for photographs expect a small tip, usually NPR 100 to 200, so ask first and pay what you agreed.

experiences.title: Bagmati evening aarti at Pashupatinath
experiences.best_time: Dusk, all year; busiest on Mondays and Saturdays
experiences.price_hint: Free to watch; guided visit ≈ ₹1,500 per person
experiences.summary: The nightly lamp ceremony on the Bagmati ghats below Pashupatinath, with priests, bells, conch shells and devotional singing for about an hour. We arrive early for a good place on the east bank terraces and explain each part of the ritual as it unfolds.
body: We reach the east bank about 45 minutes before the aarti, usually around 5:15 pm in summer and closer to 4:45 pm in December and January, when the ceremony starts earlier. That gives time to walk the riverbank, see the main temple roofs glowing in the last light from across the water and find space on the stone terraces facing the ghats. On Mondays, Saturdays, full-moon nights and during the month of Shrawan the steps fill quickly, so arriving early matters more then.

The aarti itself is led by young priests in saffron and white, each standing at a small platform on the river steps. It opens with conch shells and the ringing of bells, moves through bhajans sung by the crowd, and builds to the waving of large multi-tiered brass lamps toward the river and the temple. Cremation fires continue to burn a short way downstream throughout, which many guests find moving rather than disturbing. Devotees sing along and float small leaf-plate lamps on the river.

Anyone may watch, and non-Hindus are welcome on the terraces; only the main temple courtyard is restricted. Photography of the aarti from the east bank is generally accepted, but turn off the flash and do not point lenses at the cremation platforms. Bring a light shawl from October to March, as the stone steps cool fast after dark. The aarti lasts about an hour; timings can shift for festivals and special days, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What time does the Pashupatinath aarti start?
faqs.a: The Bagmati aarti usually starts around 6 pm from spring to autumn and about 5:30 pm in winter, following sunset. It runs for roughly an hour. Times change for festivals such as Maha Shivaratri and Teej and on special days, so we confirm the timing on the day; please check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus watch the Pashupatinath evening aarti?
faqs.a: Yes. The aarti takes place on the river steps outside the main courtyard, and everyone may watch from the terraces on the east bank of the Bagmati. Foreign visitors pay the complex entry fee of around NPR 1,000. Dress modestly, sit quietly, and follow the lead of devotees around you when they stand or sing.

faqs.q: Is the Pashupatinath aarti similar to the Ganga aarti in Varanasi?
faqs.a: It follows a similar pattern of lamps, bells, conch shells and bhajans, but it is smaller and more intimate than the Varanasi Ganga aarti. The Bagmati is a narrow river, so you sit close to the priests and the temple. Many Indian pilgrims tell us the setting, with the temple roofs behind, feels more personal.

experiences.title: Rudrabhishek puja with a Pashupatinath priest
experiences.best_time: Morning, especially Mondays and the month of Shrawan
experiences.price_hint: Puja fee set by the temple trust; we quote on request
experiences.summary: A Rudrabhishek arranged with a priest in the Pashupatinath temple premises, bathing a Shiva lingam with milk, curd, honey, ghee and Bagmati water while the Rudri hymns are recited. We book the priest, materials and timing so your family can focus on the ritual.
body: Many of our Hindu guests come to Pashupatinath for one reason: to perform a Rudrabhishek for a family wish, a health concern, a new home or the memory of a parent. We take the family's names, gotra and sankalpa in advance and book the puja through the temple's registered priests, who work under rules set by the Pashupati Area Development Trust. Mondays, Pradosh days and the month of Shrawan (July to August) are the most favoured, and those dates fill early.

On the morning, the family meets the priest in the temple premises after darshan. The puja is done on a lingam set up for the ritual, since only the temple's own chief priests touch the main Pashupati lingam. The lingam is bathed in turn with milk, curd, honey, ghee, sugar and water from the Bagmati, then dressed with bel leaves, flowers, sandalwood paste and sacred thread, while the priest recites the Rudri and leads the family through each offering. A full Rudrabhishek takes 1.5 to 2 hours.

The puja fee depends on the type of ritual and the number of priests, and the trust revises its rates; check current status before you travel. Pay through the official counter or as agreed in our quotation, never to touts at the gate. Men usually wear a kurta or dhoti and women a sari or salwar suit; no leather is allowed. Keep the morning free of plans so the ritual is not rushed, and bring a bag for the prasad you will carry home.

faqs.q: How do I book a Rudrabhishek at Pashupatinath from India?
faqs.a: Send us the date you prefer, the names and gotra of the family members and the purpose of the puja, and we book a registered priest and materials through the temple premises. Confirm at least two weeks ahead for Mondays and Shrawan, and longer for Maha Shivaratri. We send a written quote with the fee before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Rudrabhishek at Pashupatinath cost?
faqs.a: The fee varies with the form of the puja, the number of priests and the materials, and the temple trust revises its rates from time to time, so check current status before you travel. We quote the exact amount in writing before booking. Avoid anyone at the gate offering a cheaper puja, as unregistered operators are common.

faqs.q: Can women perform Rudrabhishek at Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Yes. Women take part fully in the Rudrabhishek alongside the rest of the family, making the offerings with the priest. Many families follow their own custom about participation during menstruation, and priests respect that. Modest traditional dress such as a sari or salwar suit is expected, and leather items must be left outside.

experiences.title: Pashupatinath to Guhyeshwari heritage walk
experiences.summary: A guided 3 km walk that links Pashupatinath with Guhyeshwari, the Shakti Peeth upstream on the Bagmati, through the Mrigasthali forest and its shrines. It covers the ghats, the Gorakhnath area, the deer enclosure and the river path, and pairs naturally with the evening aarti.
body: We start on the west bank below the main gate, where your guide explains the layout of the complex, the role of the Bhatta priests and the ritual life of the ghats. Hindus in the group can take darshan in the main courtyard while others wait on the east bank terraces. Crossing the footbridge, we look over Arya Ghat from a respectful distance and talk through the stages of a Hindu cremation, from washing the body in the Bagmati to the final scattering of the ashes in the river.

Steps then climb into Mrigasthali, the forest named for Shiva's legendary wanderings as a deer. The path passes rows of small lingam shrines, the Gorakhnath area with its tall trident, a quiet deer enclosure and troops of rhesus monkeys. Some temples here, including Vishwarupa, are open only to Hindus, and your guide will point out where to stay outside. From the far edge of the forest the path drops back to the Bagmati and follows the river upstream for about 1 km.

Guhyeshwari is one of the Shakti Peethas, linked to the legend of Sati's body falling across the subcontinent, and the goddess is worshipped here in the form of a sacred water vessel. The present temple is usually dated to the 17th century and the reign of Pratap Malla. Only Hindus may enter the inner courtyard; others can view the gilded canopy over the shrine from the gate. The total walk is about 3 km on stone steps and paved paths, and we can finish back at Pashupatinath for the aarti.

faqs.q: How far is Guhyeshwari from Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Guhyeshwari is about 1 km upstream of Pashupatinath along the Bagmati, roughly 15 minutes on foot by the river path or 25 to 30 minutes if you go through the Mrigasthali forest. Cars can reach Guhyeshwari by road from Gaushala and Sifal, and many pilgrims visit both temples in one morning.

No. As at Pashupatinath, only Hindus may enter the inner courtyard of Guhyeshwari, and the rule is enforced at the gate. Visitors of other faiths can see the temple from outside and walk the river path and forest around it freely. Your guide will show you the best places to stand without crowding the entrance.

faqs.q: Why is Guhyeshwari important to visit with Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Guhyeshwari is one of the Shakti Peethas, and many devotees believe a visit to Pashupatinath is complete only after paying respects to the goddess here, as Shiva and Shakti are worshipped together. Pilgrims often go to Guhyeshwari first and then to Pashupatinath. Our temple tours include both on the same morning.

Non-Hindus cannot enter the main temple courtyard, and guards check at the gates. They can still visit the rest of the complex: the east bank terraces opposite the temple, the ghats, the Mrigasthali forest and the evening aarti. Foreign visitors pay an entry fee of around NPR 1,000 for the complex; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Pashupatinath for Indians?
faqs.a: Indian and Nepali Hindus enter free for darshan in the main temple. Foreign visitors of other nationalities pay about NPR 1,000 to visit the complex, and rules for SAARC visitors have changed over the years. Puja fees are separate and set by the temple trust. Check current status before you travel, as fees are revised from time to time.

faqs.q: What are the Pashupatinath darshan timings?
faqs.a: The main temple usually opens around 4 am and closes in the evening after the rituals, around 7 pm, with the four doors of the inner shrine opened at set times during the day. Hours change on festival days and can vary by season, so check current status before you travel. Weekday mid-mornings have the shortest queues.

faqs.q: Is it respectful to watch cremations at Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Yes, if you do it quietly from the east bank. Cremations at Arya Ghat and Bhasmeshwar Ghat are public, and families accept onlookers at a distance. Do not walk onto the platforms, speak loudly, or photograph the bodies or mourners. If you feel uncomfortable, move away; your guide can explain the rites instead of you watching closely.

faqs.q: How much time do we need at Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Allow 2 to 3 hours for darshan, the ghats and the Mrigasthali forest, and 3 to 4 hours if you add the evening aarti or Guhyeshwari. Pilgrims performing a Rudrabhishek should keep the whole morning free. We usually schedule Pashupatinath in the afternoon, after Boudhanath, so the day ends with the aarti.

faqs.q: When is Maha Shivaratri at Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Maha Shivaratri falls on the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight in the month of Falgun, usually in February or early March. Hundreds of thousands of devotees and many sadhus from India attend, queues run for hours and the area closes to vehicles. Exact dates and crowd rules change each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Pashupatinath one of the 12 Jyotirlingas?
faqs.a: No, Pashupatinath is not among the twelve Jyotirlingas, but Hindus count it among the holiest Shiva shrines. By one popular tradition Shiva's head emerged in Nepal while his hump remained at Kedarnath, and Doleshwor Mahadev near Bhaktapur is honoured as that head. Our Kathmandu temple tour visits Pashupatinath and Doleshwor on the same trip.

faqs.q: How far is Pashupatinath from Kathmandu airport?
faqs.a: Pashupatinath is only about 2 km from Tribhuvan International Airport, around 15 minutes by car. That makes it easy to visit straight after landing or before an afternoon flight. If you plan a visit on your departure day, leave at least 3 hours between leaving the temple and your international flight.

faqs.q: What should I wear to Pashupatinath?
faqs.a: Wear modest clothes covering shoulders and knees: kurta, sari, salwar suit or long trousers and a shirt all work. Leather belts, wallets and bags are not allowed inside the main temple, and phones and cameras stay outside the courtyard. Shoes come off at the inner gate, so socks help on cold winter mornings.
